title: Erdős #101 — Four-Point Lines from Planar Point Sets

problemStatement.formal: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no five of which are on a line, the number of lines containing four points is $o(n^2)$.
problemStatement.plain: Given n points in the plane with no five collinear, prove that the number of lines containing exactly four of the points is o(n²).
whyMatters: Fundamental problem in combinatorial geometry connecting point-line incidences to collinearity structure
Related to the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem and its applications
The gap between best known lower bound n^{2-O(1/√(log n))} and the conjectured o(n²) upper bound is a major open question
Problem 71 on Ben Green's open problems list; $100 Erdős prize

proven: Collinearity definitions and basic properties (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity)
NoFiveCollinear predicate and vacuous case for |P| ≤ 4
noFiveCollinear_line_bound: under NoFiveCollinear, any line through 2 points has ≤ 4 points
four_collinear_unique: two 4-collinear subsets sharing 2 common collinear points must be equal
trivial_upper_bound_sq: fourPointLineCount(P) ≤ n² (injection to ordered pairs)
trivial_upper_bound: fourPointLineCount(P) ≤ n(n-1)/2 (injection to unordered pairs)
improved_upper_bound: fourPointLineCount(P) ≤ n(n-1)/12 (pair-packing via C(4,2)=6 disjoint pairs)
fourCollinearThrough_bound: at most (n-1)/3 four-point lines through any single point
Double-counting connection: per-point and global bounds are equivalent via Σ_p |FCT(p)| = 4|F|
open: Main conjecture: fourPointLineCount(P) = o(n²) — genuinely OPEN, $100 prize
Best lower bound: n^{2-O(1/√(log n))} by Solymosi-Stojaković (2013), disproving Θ(n^{3/2}) guess
Closing the gap between O(n²) and o(n²) requires genuinely new ideas beyond Szemerédi-Trotter

knowledge.progressSummary: SURVEY: Erdős #101 is a genuine OPEN problem ($100 prize). The existing Lean formalization in Erdos101Problem.lean is comprehensive and high-quality. It proves all combinatorial bounds achievable without resolving the main conjecture: trivial O(n²), improved O(n(n-1)/2), tight O(n(n-1)/12) via pair-packing, and per-point bound (n-1)/3. The double-counting connection between these is documented. The main conjecture and known lower bounds are correctly axiomatized. No further proof work is appropriate.

insights: The n(n-1)/12 bound is tight from pure combinatorial methods — further improvement requires geometric input
Szemerédi-Trotter is axiomatized but not directly applicable to close the o(n²) gap for k=4

The existing formalization correctly separates proved combinatorial bounds from the open conjecture
Double-counting approach (per-point × 4 = global × n) gives equivalent bounds but cannot break o(n²) barrier
